newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax reform set for normal parliament route.
newsitem.headline: German tax reform set for normal parliament route.

text.p: The collapse of tax reform talks between Germany's government and opposition on Wednesday spells added delay for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's drive to reduce taxes and reform the pension system.
The government had hoped to push a reform through before the summer break, but it will now have to wait until the autumn before a compromise bill can be approved by parliament, deputies said.

The talks between Kohl's centre-right coalition and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) is aimed at reaching a consensus before the reform bill is introduced into parliament, thus ensuring it could be approved with the least possible delay.

Kohl chose this unusual procedure because the main opposition party can block tax legislation thanks to its majority in the upper house of parliament, or Bundesrat, where the 16 federal states are represented.

Now that the talks have broken down, the government plans to submit its tax reform bill to the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, on Friday and vote it through with its majority there before the summer break starts on June 27.
The upper house is expected to reject this at its July 4 session, the last before its summer break.
The bill would then go to a mediation committee in September for a compromise to be worked out.
